Guided Inquiry

1 · Alice, Bella and the corridor

Let’s meet the twins. Alice stays at x = 0 while Bella runs to a marker a distance L away at speed v, turns, and runs back. Both clocks are set to zero at the start event and read out again at the single reunion event.

We’ll use natural units: c = 1, so distances are light-years and times are years. And τ means proper time — what a clock carried along a worldline itself records.

2 · The two readings at reunion

Let’s start with the big question. Bella runs out at v = 0.80c, turns at the marker, and runs back. At the reunion the two clocks are held side by side. What do you think — how do the readings compare?

Now press Play and run the trip in Alice’s frame: τA = 10.00 yr, τB = 6.00 yr, a gap of 4.00 yr.

3 · What breaks the mirror

Here’s the puzzle that gives the paradox its name. Along each straight leg, each twin measures the other’s clock running slow — that much really is symmetric. Yet the reunion readings aren’t equal. So what do you think breaks the symmetry?

4 · The turnaround, in Bella's frame

Now let’s ride along with Bella. The scene is drawn in her frame: she’s at rest and the corridor slides past. At the instant she swaps her outbound frame for the inbound one, what do you think happens to Alice’s clock?

Press Play and keep your eye on Alice’s clock at the switch; the dashed ghost shows the no-jump bookkeeping.

5 · A longer trip, the same turn

One last experiment. Hold v at 0.80c and double Alice’s trip time ΔtA from 10 yr to 20 yr. The turnaround itself is identical. Make a guess — what happens to the age difference at reunion?

Try it: set ΔtA to 20 yr with v unchanged and re-run.

6 · Maximal ageing

So here’s the big idea. Between the start event and the reunion, Alice’s straight worldline carries the greatest proper time any worldline can carry, and Bella’s bent one carries less — the principle of maximal ageing.

The turnaround selects Bella’s path rather than causing the difference; in her frame, it’s the sweep of simultaneity that supplies the time the leg-by-leg bookkeeping misses. At the current settings τA = 10.00 yr and τB = 6.00 yr.

The Physics

The twin paradox · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Alice stays put while her twin Bella runs to a marker and back, and the sim shows the trip from either twin's frame. It lets you compare what the two clocks read when the twins meet again, the standard test of what a clock measures in special relativity.

What you'll learn

  • What proper time is, and how to work it out along a path.
  • How the two clock readings at the reunion depend on Bella's speed v and the trip time ΔtA.
  • How the trip is described in each twin's rest frame, and where the two descriptions differ.
Both twins carry a clock, set to zero at the start. They are side by side again at the end.

What's on screen

  • Alice (cyan) with her clock τA above her, in years.
  • Bella (amber) with her clock τB. The small tag under each name gives that twin's speed in the current frame.
  • Turnaround pylon and the label above the corridor: the distance from the start line to the marker.
  • Status chip and banners: which frame you are in, what each twin is doing, and the moments of the turnaround and the reunion.
  • Clock readings at reunion (sidebar): the two proper times, and their difference, for your settings.
See itSet up the opening trip, paused at the start. Watch for: both twins at the start line with both clocks at zero, and the pylon L = 4.00 ly away.

03

Proper time along a path

The twins part at the start event and meet at the reunion event. Every observer agrees on these two events and on what each clock reads at the second one. A clock records its own proper time τ: the time that passes along its own worldline between them.

The trip in Alice's frame at the opening settings (v = 0.80c, ΔtA = 10 yr), as worldlines in x and t.
Units with c = 1. The interval is ds² = −dt² + dx², so dτ = √(−ds²).
  • Alice never leaves x = 0, so dx = 0 and her proper time is the time of her frame: τA = ΔtA.
  • Bella moves at constant v on each leg, so dx = v dt and dτ = dt√(1 − v²) = dt/γ. Her two legs together last ΔtA in Alice's frame.
Each twin's proper time over the whole trip.
γ is set by v alone.
See itRun the trip in Alice's frame. Watch for: the clock above Bella (B) reading less than the clock above Alice (A) as soon as the run is under way.
04

Why the two accounts differ

  • On each straight leg the accounts are symmetric. Each twin measures the other's clock running slow by the same factor 1/γ.
  • The number of inertial frames is not symmetric. Alice needs one, S, from start to reunion. Bella needs two: S′ on the way out and S″ on the way back, because she reverses at the marker.
  • Which twin is moving depends on the frame. Which worldline is straight does not: Alice's is straight in every inertial frame, Bella's has a corner in every one.
  • In Bella's frame she is at rest and the corridor slides past. The start line and the marker are at rest in Alice's frame, so Bella measures the distance between them contracted from L to L/γ, and she measures Alice's clock running slow by 1/γ.

Time dilation compares one clock with the other frame's time. It does not say which clock reads less when the clocks are brought together.

See itRedraw the trip in Bella's frame. Watch for: the label above the corridor reading L/γ = 2.40 ly, shorter than the L = 4.00 ly of Alice's frame.

What sets the size of the gap

From τA = ΔtA and τB = ΔtA/γ, the difference between the two readings at the reunion is:

The gap: how long the trip lasts, times how much slower Bella's clock runs.

  • γ depends on v alone, so at fixed v the gap is proportional to ΔtA.
  • At fixed ΔtA the gap grows with v, but it stays below the whole trip: any v < c leaves τB > 0.

06

What the frame switch does

At the opening settings, Bella's outbound leg lasts 3.00 yr on her clock. In S′ Alice's clock runs slow by 1/γ, so it advances 3.00/γ = 1.80 yr. The return leg adds another 1.80 yr: 3.60 yr in all, yet Alice's clock reads 10.00 yr at the reunion.

The same trip in Alice's coordinates. Bella's line of "now" meets Alice's worldline at 1.80 yr before the switch and 8.20 yr after it.
  • Switching from S′ to S″ changes which event on Alice's worldline Bella counts as simultaneous with her turn.
  • Alice's clock does not skip anything. The jump is in Bella's bookkeeping: the clock face in her frame shows the reading she assigns to "now".
  • The sim draws the leg-by-leg count, without the switch, as a dashed ghost clock beside Alice's clock.
The simultaneity jump, with L = vΔtA/2 the marker distance in Alice's frame. Here 1.80 + 6.40 + 1.80 = 10.00 yr.
See itRun the trip in Bella's frame at the opening settings. Watch for: at the frame switch, Alice's clock leaping from 1.80 to 8.20 yr while the dashed ghost clock carries on from 1.80 yr.
07

The straight path ages most

  • Between two events, the unaccelerated worldline records the greatest proper time. Alice's is that straight line. Any other path between the same events, Bella's included, records less (in flat spacetime).
  • This is the reverse of distance in a plane, where the straight line is the shortest. The opposite signs of the time and space terms in ds² = −dt² + dx² make the difference.
  • In this sim the turn is instantaneous and takes no time, so the gap builds up entirely along the straight legs. The turn selects Bella's path; it does not add to either clock.
  • For the same ΔtA, a higher v makes Bella's path bend more, and τB falls.
See itRaise v to 0.95c with the 10 yr trip. Watch for: τB = 3.12 yr and Δτ = 6.88 yr, against 6.00 yr and 4.00 yr at 0.80c.
08

Where it matters

  • GPS. Satellite clocks move at about 3.9 km/s, which on its own makes them run slow by about 7.2 μs a day. Gravity at orbit height acts the other way and is larger (about 46 μs a day), so the system is built with both corrections.
  • Cosmic-ray muons. A muon lives 2.2 μs on average, which is 660 m at nearly c. Made about 15 km up, with γ ≈ 20 it travels about 13 km on average, so many reach the ground. In the muon's frame it is the atmosphere that is contracted.
  • Muon storage rings. At CERN, muons circulating at γ = 29.3 lasted 29.3 times longer than at rest, agreeing with the prediction to about 0.1%.
Go deeper: small speeds
For v ≪ c, 1 − 1/γ ≈ v²/2. The numbers are for a GPS satellite's speed.
  • For everyday speeds the gap is tiny: at 5 m/s, even 80 years of running buys about 0.35 μs.
  • The 1971 Hafele–Keating experiment flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners. They differed from ground clocks by tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, as predicted once gravity and motion were both included.
09

Summary

In one line. Each clock records the proper time along its own worldline, and between the same two events the straight worldline records the most, so Bella, who must change direction, returns with less.

Key points

  • τA = ΔtA and τB = ΔtA/γ, so the gap is ΔtA(1 − 1/γ), in units where c = 1.
  • The gap is proportional to ΔtA and grows with v.
  • Each leg is symmetric, but Alice uses one inertial frame and Bella uses two.
  • The frame switch moves Bella's "now" on Alice's worldline: relabelling, not a tick of Alice's clock.

Common mix-ups

  • "Each twin sees the other's clock slow, so the readings must match." That holds on each straight leg, but Bella also changes frames.
  • "The acceleration makes Bella younger." It selects her path. The same turn on a trip twice as long gives twice the gap.
  • "Alice really ages 6.40 yr in an instant." Her clock ticks steadily. What jumps is the reading Bella assigns to "now".

Things to try on your own

  • Use the v slider to find the speed at which τB is half of τA, then check it with γ = 2.
  • In Bella's frame set v = 0.95c and note the jump in Alice's clock at the frame switch. Compare it with v²ΔtA.
  • Set v = 0.10c and compare the reunion readings with the 0.80c trip.
